newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Daiwa says maintain exposure in Hungary, Russia.
newsitem.headline: Daiwa says maintain exposure in Hungary, Russia.

text.p: Daiwa Europe Ltd suggested that investors should maintain a heavy exposure in the Russian and Hungarian stock markets but said new investment opportunities will emerge around the Black Sea.

"Daiwa...recommends a continued heavy exposure to Russia and Hungary; indeed, relative to prospects for Prague and Bratislava they could be in different solar systems," Roger Monson, chief equity strategist and Sonja Shechter, European equity strategist said.

In the June issue of Daiwa's "Equity Strategy Quarterly" Daiwa raised its recommended weighing of Russia in its eastern European portfolio to 55 percent from 45 percent, "reflecting the falling appeal of other markets," but left Hungary's weighing steady at 15 percent, the second largest after Russia.
The strategists said the Hungarian market remains the best placed in terms of fundamentals and represents the best appreciation potential among the larger, more liquid markets.
"Along with an improving economy, shares are supported by an excellent earnings record," they said, adding that Daiwa raised its year-end target for the BUX index from 6,500 points to 7,000.

Russian shares continue to be well supported, most recently by the combination of a new confidence-building reformist team in the government and a move to record low short-term interest rates and inflation, they said.
"Our outlook for the year-end Moscow Times US$ Index is now 300-325, a gain of of 10 to 20 percent from end May levels," the Monson and Shechter said.
The strategists said that pending development Daiwa will increase its allocations to Romania, Ukraine and Bulgaria.

"As we move into 1998, out of the chaos will come a new constellation of investment opportunities bordering the Black Sea, as Romania, Ukraine and Bulgaria all move to correct the worst imbalances of their economies (with IMF and EBRD help)."
"Our allocations to these markets will rise developments permit," Monson and Shechter said.
